For simplicity sake I'm going to talk about teachers but imagine any job you want here.

The issue here is the difficulty in ranking individuals. It's relatively easy to set minimum standards teachers. It becomes much harder to separate individuals within the population of teachers. We just don't have the resources or means to rank every teacher in the world along absolute lines. At a certain point the cost to do so overcomes the net gain of doing it let alone the issues with subjective evaluation. It just isn't possible to know who is going to end up being a better teacher five years from now or who will be better in superior positions (a great worker bee doesn't always make a great manager). How do you compare two teachers that teach in different states, to different demographics? Certainly you could create models for evaluation but those models carry the bias of the people who generate them. You end up with the "looks good on paper" phenomenon. In any endeavor you will find people who look really good on paper but end up being remarkably average or counter productive (because all they care about is padding the resume). The best way to counter this is through managerial/employee evaluations. This of course can open a whole different can of worms.

Why might a true meritocracy be a nightmare? Simple when people don't have a clear ceiling they can become viciously competitive (personal experience in the military here). In meritocratic systems people tend to equate their personal sense of worth to their place in the hierarchy. Some times a little inefficiency in the process creates a natural sense of perspective.

TL;DR There will always be people who are mismatched in the hierarchy for various reasons and that isn't necessarily a terrible thing.
